items.answer: (i) When you blow gently over the mixture, the light, papery peanut skins lift into the air and scatter, while the heavier kernels stay where they are. (ii) Only the removed peanut skins are blown away; the peanuts themselves remain. Activity 9.2 : Let us observe and create

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Allow it to dry and then observe it (Figure (b) and Figure (c)). Figure : A few drops of salt solution spread on thick black paper Question : (i) Do you observe some patches on the paper? (ii) What do you think is left on the paper? (iii) Where has the water disappeared?
items.answer: (i) Yes, after the solution dries, white or crystalline patches are observed on the dark paper where the drops of salt solution were placed (as shown in Figure (b) and (c)). (ii) The salt that was dissolved in the water is left on the paper. You can feel its presence. (iii) The water has evaporated. It changed from a liquid state to a gaseous state (water vapor) and mixed with the surrounding air. This is why only the salt remains behind. Activity 9.3 : Let us investigate This activity may be demonstrated by the teacher.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Allow the china dish to cool down. Question : (i) What do you observe? What is left in the china dish? (ii) Did you get the salt back?
items.answer: (i) You observe the water in the salt solution heating up, boiling, and turning into steam (water vapor), which then escapes into the air. (ii) Yes, the process of heating the solution and boiling away the water allows you to recover the salt that was originally dissolved. Activity 9.4 : Let us experiment

items.stem: Separating oil from water. 10 Separating salt from salt solution. Now, take two baskets, each representing one of the two purposes for which we separate substances. Form two teams and see who will get the maximum correct entries.
items.answer: Basket 1 : To remove any one of the components that is not useful (Removing unwanted or harmful components)

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What purpose does hand-picking serve in the process of separation? (i) Filtration (ii) Sorting (iii) Evaporation (iv) Decantation
items.answer: (ii) Sorting Hand-picking is used to sort out and remove unwanted pieces (stones, twigs, spoiled grains, etc.) from a mixture.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Which of the following substances are commonly separated using the churning method? (i) Oil from water (ii) Sand from water (iii) Cream from milk (iv) Oxygen from air
items.answer: (iii) Cream from milk Churning (or buttering) spins curd or milk so that the lighter fat (cream/butter) rises and can be skimmed off.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Which factor is usually essential for filtration? (i) Apparatus size (ii) Presence of air (iii) Pore size (iv) Temperature of the mixture
items.answer: (iii) Pore size Whether a particle passes through a filter depends on the size of the pores in the filter material.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: State True (T) or False (F). Correct each false statement. (i) Salt can be separated from salt solution by keeping it under the Sun. (ii) Hand-picking should be used only when the quantity of one component is less. (iii) A mixture of puffed rice and rice grains can be separated by threshing. (iv) A mixture of mustard oil and lemon water can be separated by decantation. (v) Sieving is used to separate a mixture of rice flour and water.
items.answer: (i) True, Sunlight heats the solution; water evaporates, leaving salt crystals (evaporation). (ii) True, The method is practical only when the unwanted component is present in a small amount. (iii) False, Correct : It can be separated by winnowing (blowing air) or hand-picking, not threshing (which separates grains from stalks). (iv) True, Oil and water form two layers; the upper oil layer can be decanted or removed with a separating funnel. (v) False, Correct : Filtration (using filter paper or muslin) separates flour from water; sieving works only for dry solids of different sizes.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: In what situations would you use decantation instead of filtration to separate solids from liquids?
items.answer: Use decantation (simply pouring off the clear liquid) when:

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Can you relate the presence of nasal hair to any separation process?
items.answer: Yes. Nasal hairs work like a natural filter : as air passes through our nose, the hairs trap dust, pollen and other large particles while letting the clean air move on to the lungs. This is similar to the filtration method of separation, where a filter medium holds back solid impurities and allows the fluid to pass through.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: During the COVID-19 pandemic, all of us wore masks. Generally, what material are they made of? What is the role of these masks?
items.answer: Material : Most medical (surgical) masks are made of thin, non-woven plastic fibres called polypropylene. Simple reusable masks are usually made of tightly woven cotton cloth in two or three layers. Role : The mask works like a tiny filter. It traps the saliva droplets we breathe, talk, cough or sneeze out, so fewer germs reach other people, and it also blocks many droplets in the air from reaching our own nose and mouth. In this way masks help slow the spread of viruses such as COVID-19.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: A mixture containing potatoes, salt and sawdust has been given to you. Outline a stepwise procedure for separating each component from this mixture.
items.answer: 1. Hand-pick potatoes and set them aside.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Read the following story titled ‘Intelligent Leela’ and tick the most appropriate options. Provide a suitable title of your choice for the paragraph. Leela was working in the farm with her father when she realized that they left their drinking water at home. Before her father felt thirsty/ hungry, she went to the nearby pond to fetch some water/grains. After obtaining some water in the container, she noticed that the water was muddy and fit/unfit for drinking. To purify the water, she kept it for some time and then she filtered/churned the muddy water using a piece of paper/muslin cloth. Leela, then, cooled/boiled the water for about 10 minutes in a covered pan. After cooling/boiling, she filtered/churned ita gain and made it fit/unfit for drinking. She served this water other father while having food, who blessed her and appreciated her efforts.
items.answer: Paragraph with the correct words filled in Leela was working in the farm with her father when she realized that they had left their drinking water at home. Before her father felt thirsty, she went to the nearby pond to fetch some water. After obtaining some water in the container, she noticed that it was muddy and unfit for drinking. To purify it, she kept the water for a while and then filtered it through a piece of muslin cloth. Leela then boiled the water for about ten minutes in a covered pan. After cooling, she filtered it once more and made it fit to drink. She served the water to her father during their meal, and he blessed her for her thoughtful effort.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is handpicking as a method of separation?

options.label: A
options.text: Separating substances using a sieve

options.label: B
options.text: Picking substances by hand from a mixture based on differences in size, color, or shape

options.label: C
options.text: Using a magnet to separate magnetic materials

options.label: D
options.text: Allowing heavier particles to settle down in water

items.answer: (B) Picking substances by hand from a mixture based on differences in size, color, or shape. Handpicking is a simple separation method where undesirable components are manually removed from a mixture. This is effective when there are visible differences in size, color, or shape between the components.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: In the story, what were Malli’s Nani and other community members separating from grains by handpicking?

options.label: A
options.text: Different types of grains from each other

options.label: B
options.text: Small stones and husk from the grains

options.label: C
options.text: Larger grains from smaller grains

options.label: D
options.text: Colored grains from white grains

items.answer: (B) Small stones and husk from the grains. Malli and Valli observed their relatives handpicking to remove unwanted small stones and pieces of husk from the harvested grains to make them fit for cooking.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: When is handpicking a convenient method of separation?

options.label: A
options.text: When the particles to be removed are very small and numerous

options.label: B
options.text: When the particles to be removed are present in small quantities and are easily picked by hand

options.label: C
options.text: When all components of the mixture are identical in appearance

options.label: D
options.text: When the mixture is a liquid

items.answer: (B) When the particles to be removed are present in small quantities and are easily picked by hand. Handpicking is practical if the unwanted particles are few, relatively large, and visually distinct, allowing for easy manual removal without excessive time or effort.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is threshing?

options.label: A
options.text: The process of grinding grains into flour

options.label: B
options.text: The process of separating grains from the stalks by beating

options.label: C
options.text: The process of separating husk from grains using wind

options.label: D
options.text: The process of handpicking stones from grains

items.answer: (B) The process of separating grains from the stalks by beating. Threshing is the method used to detach edible grains from their harvested stalks or chaff, traditionally done by beating the stalks against a hard surface or by using animals or machines.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What happens when roasted peanuts are rubbed between palms and then blown upon?

options.label: A
options.text: The peanuts become softer and easier to eat

options.label: B
options.text: The heavier peanuts are blown away, leaving the skins

options.label: C
options.text: The lighter peanut skins are blown away, separating them from the heavier peanuts

options.label: D
options.text: Both peanuts and skins stick together and cannot be separated by blowing

items.answer: (C) The lighter peanut skins are blown away, separating them from the heavier peanuts. Rubbing loosens the skins from the peanuts. When blown, the lighter skins are carried away by the air, while the heavier peanuts remain, demonstrating a simple separation based on weight.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: The method of winnowing is based on what principle to separate components of a mixture?

options.label: A
options.text: Difference in color of the components

options.label: B
options.text: Difference in size of the components

options.label: C
options.text: Difference in weight, where lighter components are blown away by wind or air

options.label: D
options.text: Difference in magnetic properties of the components

items.answer: (C) Difference in weight, where lighter components are blown away by wind or air. Winnowing utilizes wind or blowing air to separate lighter components (like husk or chaff) from heavier components (like grains). The lighter particles are carried away, leaving the heavier ones behind.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is sieving used for?

options.label: A
options.text: Separating dissolved solids from a liquid

options.label: B
options.text: Separating magnetic substances from non- magnetic ones

options.label: C
options.text: Separating components of a solid-solid mixture that have different sizes using a sieve

options.label: D
options.text: Separating heavier components from lighter ones using wind

items.answer: (C) Separating components of a solid-solid mixture that have different sizes using a sieve. Sieving employs a sieve (a mesh or perforated surface) to separate solid particles of different sizes. Smaller particles pass through the holes, while larger ones are retained.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: How is common salt primarily obtained from seawater, as described ?

options.label: A
options.text: By filtering the seawater through large sieves

options.label: B
options.text: By allowing seawater to evaporate in shallow pits, leaving behind solid salt

options.label: C
options.text: By boiling the seawater and collecting the condensed steam

options.label: D
options.text: By adding chemicals to seawater that precipitate the salt

items.answer: (B) By allowing seawater to evaporate in shallow pits, leaving behind solid salt. Salt is obtained from seawater by collecting the water in shallow pits and allowing the sun and wind to evaporate the water. The dissolved salts are left behind as a solid mixture.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: In Activity 9.2, when a salt solution is spread on dark paper and allowed to dry, what is left behind on the paper?

options.label: A
options.text: Only water stains

options.label: B
options.text: Patches of salt, as the water evaporates

options.label: C
options.text: The paper turns completely black

options.label: D
options.text: Nothing is left behind as both salt and water evaporate

items.answer: (B) Patches of salt, as the water evaporates. When the salt solution dries, the water component changes into vapour (evaporates) and escapes into the air. The dissolved salt, being a solid, remains on the paper as patches.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is sedimentation?

options.label: A
options.text: The process of pouring out a liquid without disturbing the settled solids

options.label: B
options.text: The process of separating solids from a liquid using a filter

options.label: C
options.text: The process of settling down of heavier insoluble components at the bottom of a liquid

options.label: D
options.text: The process of converting a liquid into its vapour

items.answer: (C) The process of settling down of heavier insoluble components at the bottom of a liquid. Sedimentation occurs when a mixture of a liquid and insoluble heavier solids is left undisturbed. The heavier solid particles gradually settle down to the bottom of the container.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: In the context of making tea, what method does Dada first suggest for removing most tea leaves if a strainer is not available?

options.label: A
options.text: Filtration using a cloth

options.label: B
options.text: Magnetic separation

options.label: C
options.text: Decantation after allowing tea leaves to settle

options.label: D
options.text: Evaporation of the tea

items.answer: (C) Decantation after allowing tea leaves to settle. Dada explains that if a strainer isn’t available, one can leave the tea undisturbed for some time (sedimentation of tea leaves) and then gently pour the tea into a cup (decantation).

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Why might decantation not completely separate all tea leaves from tea?

options.label: A
options.text: Because tea leaves are soluble in hot tea

options.label: B
options.text: Because some finer tea leaves might remain suspended or get poured along with the liquid

options.label: C
options.text: Because decantation only works for separating liquids from liquids

options.label: D
options.text: Because the tea is too hot for complete separation

items.answer: (B) Because some finer tea leaves might remain suspended or get poured along with the liquid. While heavier tea leaves settle, some smaller or lighter particles may remain suspended in the tea or get disturbed and poured out with the liquid during decantation, making the separation incomplete.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is filtration?

options.label: A
options.text: The process of beating stalks to separate grains

options.label: B
options.text: The process of separating insoluble solid components from a liquid using a filter

options.label: C
options.text: The process of separating substances based on their weight using wind

options.label: D
options.text: The process of allowing heavier particles to settle in a liquid

items.answer: (B) The process of separating insoluble solid components from a liquid using a filter. Filtration involves passing a mixture of a liquid and insoluble solids through a filter (like a strainer, cloth or filter paper). The liquid passes through, while the solid particles are retained by the filter.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What material, with very fine pores, is mentioned as being a more effective filter than a cloth for separating fine impurities from muddy water?

options.label: A
options.text: A metal sieve

options.label: B
options.text: A plastic mesh

options.label: C
options.text: Filter paper

options.label: D
options.text: A bamboo tray

items.answer: (C) Filter paper Filter paper has extremely fine pores that can trap very small insoluble particles, making it more effective than a cloth for separating fine impurities like mud from water.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: How does filtration using a filter paper differ from sieving wheat flour?

options.label: A
options.text: Filtration separates two solids; sieving separates a solid from a liquid

options.label: B
options.text: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; sieving separates solid particles of different sizes

options.label: C
options.text: Filtration uses large pores; sieving uses very fine pores

options.label: D
options.text: Filtration always uses heat; sieving is done at room temperature

items.answer: (B) Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; sieving separates solid particles of different sizes. Filtration is used to separate undissolved solids from a liquid (e.g., mud from water). Sieving is used to separate solid components of different particle sizes from each other (e.g., bran from flour).

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: A fisherman casts a net into the water. Water drains out through the mesh of the net, while fish are caught. This method of catching fish is somewhat similar to which separation technique?

options.label: A
options.text: Evaporation

options.label: B
options.text: Sedimentation

options.label: C
options.text: Filtration

options.label: D
options.text: Magnetic separation

items.answer: (C) Filtration The fishing net acts like a filter. It allows the water (liquid) to pass through its mesh while retaining the larger fish (solid components), similar to how a filter separates solids from liquids.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is churning primarily used for, as described?

options.label: A
options.text: To separate stones from rice

options.label: B
options.text: To separate butter from curd or cream

options.label: C
options.text: To separate salt from seawater

options.label: D
options.text: To separate husk from grains

items.answer: (B) To separate butter from curd or cream. Churning is the process of vigorously agitating curd or cream. This agitation causes the lighter butterfat particles to clump together and separate from the liquid buttermilk.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: When churning curd, what happens to the butter and buttermilk?

options.label: A
options.text: Butter settles at the bottom, and buttermilk floats

options.label: B
options.text: Butter, being lighter, floats at the top, while buttermilk is left behind

options.label: C
options.text: Both mix uniformly and cannot be separated by churning

options.label: D
options.text: Buttermilk evaporates, leaving solid butter

items.answer: (B) Butter, being lighter, floats at the top, while buttermilk is left behind. During the churning process, the lighter butterfat coagulates and floats on the surface of the heavier liquid, which is the buttermilk.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Why can a magnet be used to separate iron nails from sawdust?

options.label: A
options.text: Because sawdust is magnetic, and iron nails are not

options.label: B
options.text: Because iron nails are magnetic and are attracted to the magnet, while sawdust is non-magnetic

options.label: C
options.text: Because both iron nails and sawdust are attracted to magnets equally

options.label: D
options.text: Because magnets repel sawdust and attract iron nails

items.answer: (B) Because iron nails are magnetic and are attracted to the magnet, while sawdust is non- magnetic. Iron is a magnetic material, meaning it is attracted to magnets. Sawdust is non-magnetic. Therefore, when a magnet is moved through the mixture, it will pick up the iron nails, leaving the sawdust behind.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is magnetic separation?

options.label: A
options.text: Separating substances based on their color using magnets

options.label: B
options.text: Separating magnetic and non-magnetic substances from a mixture using a magnet

options.label: C
options.text: Using magnets to dissolve substances in water

options.label: D
options.text: Breaking magnets into smaller pieces

items.answer: (B) Separating magnetic and non-magnetic substances from a mixture using a magnet. Magnetic separation is a method that utilizes the property of magnetism to separate materials that are attracted to a magnet (magnetic) from those that are not (non-magnetic).

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is the traditional tool of ten used by farmers for winnowing grains, as shown in Figure

options.label: A
options.text: A metal sieve

options.label: B
options.text: ? Figure : (a) Bamboo tray Figure : (b) Winnowing

options.label: C
options.text: A soop (bamboo tray)

options.label: D
options.text: A threshing machine

items.answer: (C) A soop (bamboo tray) A soop is a traditional winnowing tray, usually made of bamboo, used to separate husk from grains by allowing the wind to blow the lighter husk away.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is the main difference between threshing and winnowing? larger impurities; winnowing separates smaller ones.

options.label: A
options.text: Threshing separates grains from stalks; winnowing separates husk from grains

options.label: B
options.text: Threshing uses wind; winnowing involves beating

options.label: C
options.text: Threshing is done by hand; winnowing always requires machines

options.label: D
options.text: Threshing separates

items.answer: (A) Threshing separates grains from stalks; winnowing separates husk from grains. Threshing is the process of detaching the grains from the harvested plant stalks. Winnowing is the subsequent process of separating the lighter husk or chaff from these threshed grains using air currents.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Which of the following methods would NOT be suitable for separating a mixture of salt dissolved in water to recover both salt and water?

options.label: A
options.text: Evaporation followed by condensation

options.label: B
options.text: Simple evaporation (if only salt is needed)

options.label: C
options.text: Filtration

options.label: D
options.text: Distillation (a more advanced form of evaporation and condensation)

items.answer: (C) Filtration. Salt dissolves in water to form a solution. Filtration is used to separate insoluble solids from liquids, so it would not be effective in separating dissolved salt from water. Evaporation and condensation can recover both.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: If you have a mixture of sand and sugar, and you add water to it and stir, how can you then separate the sugar from the sand?

options.label: A
options.text: By handpicking the sugar crystals

options.label: B
options.text: By using a magnet to attract the sugar

options.label: C
options.text: By decantation/filtration (to remove sand) followed by evaporation (to recover sugar from solution)

options.label: D
options.text: By winnowing the wet mixture

items.answer: (C) By decantation/filtration (to remove sand) followed by evaporation (to recover sugar from solution). Sugar will dissolve in water, but sand will not. The sand can be separated by decantation or filtration. Then, the sugar can be recovered from the sugar-water solution by evaporating the water.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Assertion (A) : Sieving can be used to separate flour from bran. Reason (R) : Flour particles are smaller and pass through the sieve, while larger bran particles are retained.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Sieving separates components based on particle size. In the case of flour and bran, the finer flour particles can pass through the mesh of a sieve, while the coarser bran particles remain on top.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Mami is preparing meethi puri and wants to remove any coarse particles or impurities from the wheat flour before kneading it. Which method of separation would be most appropriate for Mami to use?

options.label: A
options.text: Winnowing

options.label: B
options.text: Sieving

options.label: C
options.text: Sedimentation

options.label: D
options.text: Evaporation

items.answer: (B) Sieving To separate coarser particles (like bran or small stones) from fine wheat flour, sieving is the ideal method. The fine flour will pass through the sieve, while the larger impurities will be retained.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: According to Kabir’s doha (couplet), what action does a soop (winnowing fan) perform with grains and husk?

options.label: A
options.text: It mixes them together thoroughly

options.label: B
options.text: It retains the husk and lets the grains blow away

options.label: C
options.text: It lets the husk blow away while retaining the grains

options.label: D
options.text: It grinds both grains and husk into powder

items.answer: (C) It lets the husk blow away while retaining the grains. The doha uses the analogy of a winnowing fan (soop) which separates the undesirable husk (letting it blow away) from the valuable grains (retaining them), just as wise people retain virtues and discard vices.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Why is it important to remove stones from grains before cooking?

options.label: A
options.text: Stones add a unique flavor to the food

options.label: B
options.text: Stones make the food easier to digest

options.label: C
options.text: Stones are inedible, can damage teeth, and make the food unfit for consumption

options.label: D
options.text: Stones help the grains cook faster

items.answer: (C) Stones are inedible, can damage teeth, and make the food unfit for consumption. Stones are hard, inedible impurities. If present in food, they can be unpleasant to eat, potentially damage teeth, and generally make the food unsafe or undesirable.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: The liquid that is poured out after sedimentation, leaving the settled solids behind, is part of which process?

options.label: A
options.text: Filtration

options.label: B
options.text: Evaporation

options.label: C
options.text: Decantation

options.label: D
options.text: Churning

items.answer: (C) Decantation Decantation is the process of carefully pouring off the liquid from a mixture after the heavier, insoluble solid particles have settled at the bottom through sedimentation.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: In the Arrived system mentioned, why are herbs or parts of plants often dried in the shade?

options.label: A
options.text: To enhance their color and fragrance

options.label: B
options.text: To facilitate the evaporation of excess water, leaving behind the medicinal components

options.label: C
options.text: To protect them from insects and pests

options.label: D
options.text: To make them easier to grind into a powder

items.answer: (B) To facilitate the evaporation of excess water, leaving behind the medicinal components. Drying medicinal plants in the shade helps to slowly remove excess moisture through evaporation. This concentrates the active medicinal compounds and aids in preservation.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is a key difference between the residue and the filtrate obtained after filtration?

options.label: A
options.text: Residue is the liquid that passes through; filtrate is the solid retained

options.label: B
options.text: Residue is the solid retained on the filter; filtrate is the liquid that passes through

options.label: C
options.text: Both residue and filtrate are solids of different sizes

options.label: D
options.text: Both residue and filtrate are liquids of different clarity

items.answer: (B) Residue is the solid retained on the filter; filtrate is the liquid that passes through. In filtration, the insoluble solid particles that are trapped and remain on the filter medium (like filter paper) are called the residue. The clear liquid that passes through the filter is called the filtrate.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Which of these separation methods would be LEAST effective for separating a mixture of oil and water?

options.label: A
options.text: Decantation (after allowing them to separate into layers)

options.label: B
options.text: Using a separating funnel (a specialized decantation device)

options.label: C
options.text: Sieving

options.label: D
options.text: Allowing the oil to float and skimming it off

items.answer: (C) Sieving Oil and water are immiscible liquids that form separate layers. Decantation or a separating funnel can be used. Sieving is for separating solids of different sizes or solids from liquids, not two immiscible liquids.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: A construction worker needs to separate small pebbles and stones from a heap of sand to make fine mortar. Which method would be most suitable?

options.label: A
options.text: Winnowing

options.label: B
options.text: Handpicking (if pebbles are few and large) or Sieving (if pebbles are many and smaller)

options.label: C
options.text: Magnetic separation

options.label: D
options.text: Evaporation

items.answer: (B) Handpicking (if pebbles are few and large) or Sieving (if pebbles are many and smaller) If the pebbles are relatively large and not too numerous, handpicking might be feasible. However, for a larger quantity or smaller pebbles mixed with sand, sieving with an appropriate mesh size would be more efficient.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Assertion (A) : Modern threshing machines can perform both threshing and winnowing simultaneously. Reason (R) : These machines are designed to beat grains from stalks and then use air currents to separate the lighter husk.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Modern combine harvesters and threshers are engineered to first separate grains from the stalks (threshing) and then immediately use built-in fans or air blowers to remove the lighter chaff and husk (winnowing).

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Farmers beating stalks to separate grains.

options.label: A
options.text: 1 and 2 only

options.label: B
options.text: 2 and 3 only

options.label: C
options.text: 1 and 3 only

items.answer: (C) 1 and 3 only Malli separating peppers is handpicking. Farmers beating stalks is threshing. Kneading flour is a process of mixing and preparation, not separation of existing components.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: In a science experiment, students mix chalk powder with water. After stirring, the chalk powder gradually settles at the bottom of the beaker. The process of chalk powder settling is called (I)__________, and pouring off the water is called (II)__________.

options.label: A
options.text: (I) Filtration, (II) Evaporation

options.label: B
options.text: (I) Sedimentation, (II) Decantation

options.label: C
options.text: (I) Sieving, (II) Churning

options.label: D
options.text: (I) Condensation, (II) Threshing

items.answer: (B) (I) Sedimentation, (II) Decantation Chalk powder is insoluble and heavier than water, so it settles down (sedimentation). The careful pouring of the clearer liquid from the top, without disturbing the settled solid, is decantation.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Why is it that when salt dissolves in water, it seems to disappear, but when sand is mixed with water, it remains visible?

options.label: A
options.text: Salt is lighter than sand

options.label: B
options.text: Salt is soluble in water, meaning its particles spread out uniformly; sand is insoluble

options.label: C
options.text: Salt reacts chemically with water; sand does not

options.label: D
options.text: Water evaporates faster from a salt solution than from a sand mixture

items.answer: (B) Salt is soluble in water, meaning its particles spread out uniformly; sand is insoluble. Soluble substances like salt break down into very tiny particles that disperse evenly throughout the water, making them invisible. Insoluble substances like sand do not dissolve and their larger particles remain visible.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: The process of separating insoluble particles that get filtered out and remain on the filter paper is known as the:

options.label: A
options.text: Filtrate

options.label: B
options.text: Solution

options.label: C
options.text: Residue

options.label: D
options.text: Sediment

items.answer: (C) Residue When a mixture is filtered, the insoluble solid material that is caught by and remains on the filter (e.g., filter paper) is termed the residue.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What did Malli and Valli observe a group of farmers doing with harvested wheat stalks in the fields?

options.label: A
options.text: Grinding them into flour

options.label: B
options.text: Soaking them in water

options.label: C
options.text: Beating the stalks on a large wooden log

options.label: D
options.text: Weaving them into mats

items.answer: (C) Beating the stalks on a large wooden log. The chapter describes Malli and Valli seeing farmers beating wheat stalks on a wooden log. This action is part of the threshing process to separate the grains from the stalks.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: If Valli is unable to separate husk from rice in a closed room using winnowing, what is the most likely reason?

options.label: A
options.text: The rice grains are too heavy

options.label: B
options.text: The husk is too sticky

options.label: C
options.text: There is no wind or blowing air to carry the lighter husk away

options.label: D
options.text: The room is too dark to see the components properly

items.answer: (C) There is no wind or blowing air to carry the lighter husk away. Winnowing relies on wind or a current of air to separate lighter components (like husk) from heavier ones (like rice grains). In a closed room without airflow, this method will be ineffective.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What are threshers as mentioned in the More to know! box?

options.label: A
options.text: Traditional bamboo trays used for sieving

options.label: B
options.text: Machines used for separating grains from stalks and husk, performing threshing and winnowing

options.label: C
options.text: Handheld tools for beating small quantities of grains

options.label: D
options.text: Large containers used for storing threshed grains

items.answer: (B) Machines used for separating grains from stalks and husk, performing threshing and winnowing. The More to know box explains that threshers are technological advancements—machines that perform both the task of separating grains from stalks (threshing) and separating husk from grains (winnowing) simultaneously.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Before making meethi puri, Valli’s Mami needed to remove bran from the wheat flour. Which method did she use for this?

options.label: A
options.text: Handpicking

options.label: B
options.text: Winnowing

options.label: C
options.text: Sieving

options.label: D
options.text: Sedimentation

items.answer: (C) Sieving Mami explains that a sieve is used to remove bran from flour. Sieving allows the fine flour particles to pass through while retaining the larger bran particles on the sieve.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: How does the size of particles that pass through a sieve compare to the size of particles that remain on the sieve?

options.label: A
options.text: Particles that pass through are larger than those that remain

options.label: B
options.text: Particles that pass through are the same size as those that remain

options.label: C
options.text: Particles that pass through are smaller than those that remain on the sieve

options.label: D
options.text: Size does not matter in the process of sieving

items.answer: (C) Particles that pass through are smaller than those that remain on the sieve. A sieve works by having holes of a specific size. Smaller particles can pass through these holes, while larger particles are too big and are therefore retained on the surface of the sieve.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Which of the following methods of separation would be LEAST suitable for separating tea leaves from prepared tea?

options.label: A
options.text: Filtration using a strainer

options.label: B
options.text: Decantation after sedimentation

options.label: C
options.text: Evaporation

options.label: D
options.text: Using a filter paper

items.answer: (C) Evaporation. Filtration (with a strainer or filter paper) and decantation are suitable for separating tea leaves (solid) from tea (liquid). Evaporation would remove the water component, leaving behind concentrated tea solids, which is not the desired outcome for this purpose.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: If you have a mixture of chalk powder and water, and you want to obtain clear water, which method would be most effective after allowing the chalk powder to settle?

options.label: A
options.text: Churning the mixture vigorously

options.label: B
options.text: Adding more chalk powder

options.label: C
options.text: Carefully pouring off the clear water (decantation) or filtering the mixture

options.label: D
options.text: Heating the mixture to dissolve the chalk powder

items.answer: (C) Carefully pouring off the clear water (decantation) or filtering the mixture. Chalk powder is insoluble in water and will settle (sedimentation). After settling, the clear water can be separated by decantation or, for a cleaner separation, by filtration which will trap the chalk particles.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Assertion (A) : Common salt can be obtained from seawater by evaporation. Reason (R) : Seawater contains dissolved salts, and when water evaporates, the salts are left behind as solids.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Seawater is a solution of various salts in water. The process of evaporation removes the water (as vapour), leaving the dissolved salts to crystallize and remain as a solid residue.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Sieving separates substances based on their solubility.

options.label: A
options.text: 1 only

options.label: B
options.text: 2 only

options.label: C
options.text: 1 and 3 only

options.label: D
options.text: 2 and 3 only

items.answer: (A) 1 only Handpicking relies on visible differences. Winnowing uses differences in weight and the effect of wind. Sieving separates based on particle size, not solubility. Therefore, only statement 1 is correct.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: A chef accidentally spills some iron filings into a container of sugar. Which method of separation would be quickest and most effective?

options.label: A
options.text: Dissolving the sugar in water and filtering out the iron filings

options.label: B
options.text: Using a magnet to attract and remove the iron filings

options.label: C
options.text: Carefully handpicking each iron filing

options.label: D
options.text: Sieving the mixture through a fine mesh

items.answer: (B) Using a magnet to attract and remove the iron filings. Iron filings are magnetic, while sugar is not. A magnet can easily attract and lift the iron filings out of the sugar, providing a quick and clean separation.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: When a salt solution in a china dish is heated until all water boils away, what is observed in the china dish after it cools down?

options.label: A
options.text: The china dish is empty

options.label: B
options.text: A layer of black carbon

options.label: C
options.text: Solid salt is left behind

options.label: D
options.text: A clear, odorless liquid

items.answer: (C) Solid salt is left behind. When the water in a salt solution is completely evaporated by heating, the dissolved salt, which does not evaporate, remains in the dish as a solid residue.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Why is a filter paper generally more effective than a piece of cloth for filtering very fine mud particles from water?

options.label: A
options.text: Filter paper is thicker and stronger than cloth

options.label: B
options.text: Filter paper has much finer pores than the weave of a cloth

options.label: C
options.text: Filter paper actively absorbs mud particles

options.label: D
options.text: Cloth tends to dissolve in muddy water

items.answer: (B) Filter paper has much finer pores than the weave of a cloth. Filter paper is specifically manufactured to have very small, uniform pores. These fine pores are capable of trapping much smaller particles, like fine mud, compared to the larger gaps between the threads in a piece of woven cloth.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is a mixture?

options.label: A
options.text: A pure substance with a fixed composition

options.label: B
options.text: A combination of two or more substances that are not chemically bonded

options.label: C
options.text: A substance that cannot be broken down into simpler parts

options.label: D
options.text: A liquid that can dissolve other substances

items.answer: (B) A combination of two or more substances that are not chemically bonded. The separating components from various combinations like grains and stones, or salt and water. These are examples of mixtures, where different substances are physically combined but retain their individual properties.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Which of these locations is mentioned as a place where Malli and Valli’s family uses handpicking to clean grains?

options.label: A
options.text: Ahmedabad, Gujarat

options.label: B
options.text: Puducherry

options.label: C
options.text: Nani’s house in Haryana

options.label: D
options.text: Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh

items.answer: (C) Nani’s house in Haryana The story begins with Malli and Valli visiting their Nani’s house in Haryana, where they observe community members, including their Mami and Mama, handpicking stones and husk from grains.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: How does the process of obtaining salt from seawater primarily differ from separating tea leaves from tea using a strainer?

options.label: A
options.text: Salt extraction involves evaporation; tea separation involves filtration

options.label: B
options.text: Salt extraction is a chemical change; tea separation is a physical change

options.label: C
options.text: Salt extraction removes a liquid from a solid; tea separation removes a solid from a liquid

options.label: D
options.text: Salt extraction uses magnets; tea separation uses sieves

items.answer: (A) Salt extraction involves evaporation; tea separation involves filtration. Obtaining salt from seawater relies on evaporating the water to leave the dissolved solid salt behind. Separating tea leaves from liquid tea using a strainer is a form of filtration, where insoluble solids are separated from a liquid.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a reason why we separate substances from a mixture, as implied by the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: To remove undesirable or harmful components

options.label: B
options.text: To obtain two or more different but useful components

options.label: C
options.text: To change the chemical properties of the substances

options.label: D
options.text: To make substances fit for consumption or use

items.answer: (C) To change the chemical properties of the substances. The methods of separation discussed (handpicking, sieving, evaporation, etc.) are physical methods that separate components based on their physical properties. They do not typically aim to cause chemical transformations in the substances themselves.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: A gardener has a mixture of soil and larger pebbles. To prepare fine soil for potting small seedlings, which separation method would be most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Winnowing

options.label: B
options.text: Sieving

options.label: C
options.text: Magnetic separation

options.label: D
options.text: Decantation

items.answer: (B) Sieving Sieving the mixture through a mesh of appropriate size will allow the fine soil particles to pass through while retaining the larger pebbles on the sieve.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Assertion (A) : When churning curd, butter separates from buttermilk. Reason (R) : Butter is lighter than buttermilk and floats to the top during agitation.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The process of churning causes the fat globules in curd to coalesce and form butter. Since butter (fat) is less dense (lighter) than the remaining liquid (buttermilk), it rises to the surface.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: At a construction site, a large electromagnet is used to lift and move scrap iron from a pile of rubble containing wood, concrete, and plastic. This process is an industrial application of:

options.label: A
options.text: Sieving

options.label: B
options.text: Winnowing

options.label: C
options.text: Magnetic separation

options.label: D
options.text: Filtration

items.answer: (C) Magnetic separation Iron is a magnetic material. Using an electromagnet to attract and separate it from a mixture of non- magnetic materials like wood, concrete, and plastic is a clear example of magnetic separation on a large scale.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is the method of picking out small stones from grains by hand called?
items.answer: This method is called handpicking.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: On what basis are particles separated during handpicking?
items.answer: Particles are separated based on differences in size, colour and shape.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is the process of separating grains from stalks by beating them called?
items.answer: This process is known as threshing.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Name the traditional tool, often made of bamboo, used for winnowing.
items.answer: A soop (bamboo tray) is used for winnowing.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What principle is used in winnowing to separate husk from grains?
items.answer: Winnowing separates heavier components from lighter components using wind or blowing air.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What are modern machines called that perform both threshing and winnowing?
items.answer: These machines are called threshers.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is the purpose of using a sieve when preparing flour?
items.answer: A sieve is used to remove bran or small stones from the flour.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Sieving is used when components of a mixture have different what?
items.answer: Sieving is used when components of a solid-solid mixture have different sizes.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: How is common salt traditionally obtained from seawater?
items.answer: Seawater is kept in shallow pits; water evaporates leaving behind solid salt.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is the term for a liquid in which a solid has dissolved to form a mixture?
items.answer: It is called a solution.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: In Ayurveda, how are herbs or plant parts often prepared to remove excess water?
items.answer: They are often dried in the shade, which facilitates evaporation of excess water.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is the process of settling down of heavier insoluble components at the bottom of a liquid called?
items.answer: This process is called sedimentation.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is the process of removing the clear liquid above settled impurities by tilting the vessel called?
items.answer: This process is called decantation.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Name the method used to separate tea leaves from prepared tea using a tea-strainer.
items.answer: This method is called filtration.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What material, having very fine pores, is mentioned as a filter besides cloth?
items.answer: Filter paper is mentioned as a filter with very fine pores.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is the solid material left on the filter paper after filtration called?
items.answer: The solid material left on the filter paper is called residue.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is the clear liquid obtained after filtering muddy water called?
items.answer: The clear liquid obtained is called filtrate.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What method is used to separate butter from curd using a mathni (churner)?
items.answer: The method used is churning.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What property of iron allows it to be separated from sawdust using a magnet?
items.answer: Iron is a magnetic substance, meaning it is attracted to a magnet.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is the separation of magnetic and non- magnetic substances using a magnet called?
items.answer: This method is called magnetic separation.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: When is the handpicking method most convenient for separating substances?
items.answer: Handpicking is convenient when the particles to be removed are present in small quantities and are easily distinguishable by size, colour, or shape to be picked by hand.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Explain the process of threshing as traditionally done by farmers.
items.answer: Threshing involves farmers beating harvested stalks of crops, like wheat, on a hard surface, such as a wooden log, to separate the grains from the stalks.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: How does winnowing help in separating husk from threshed wheat grains?
items.answer: In winnowing, a mixture of husk and grains is dropped from a height. The lighter husk is carried away by wind or blowing air, while the heavier grains fall down.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is the principle behind using a sieve for separation? Give an example of its use.
items.answer: Sieving separates solid components of different sizes. Finer particles pass through the sieve’s holes, while larger particles remain on it. Example: separating bran from flour.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: How is evaporation used to obtain salt from seawater?
items.answer: Seawater, a solution of salt in water, is collected in shallow pits. Sunlight and air cause the water to evaporate, leaving behind solid salt.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Briefly describe the process of sedimentation.
items.answer: Sedimentation is the process where heavier, insoluble components in a liquid mixture settle down at the bottom of the container when left undisturbed for some time.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Briefly describe the process of decantation that follows sedimentation.
items.answer: After sedimentation, decantation is the gentle pouring out of the clear liquid from the top, leaving the settled solid impurities behind in the original container.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: How can a mixture of oil and water be separated?
items.answer: Since oil and water do not mix and oil forms a separate layer (usually on top), they can be separated by decantation after allowing them to settle.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is filtration? How does a tea strainer work as a filter?
items.answer: Filtration is separating insoluble solid components from a liquid using a filter. A tea strainer has small holes that allow liquid tea to pass through while retaining the solid tea leaves.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Why can a piece of cloth be used as a filter?
items.answer: A piece of cloth can be used as a filter because it has very small holes or pores between its woven threads that can trap solid particles.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Name two materials, other than filter paper and cloth, that can be used as filters.
items.answer: Cotton and sand (or charcoal) can be used as filters. The choice depends on the particle size to be removed.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Explain the process of churning to obtain butter from curd.
items.answer: Curd is vigorously agitated (churned) using a churner (mathni). This causes the lighter butter to separate and float on top, while the buttermilk is left behind.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: How are magnets used by recyclers to separate materials from a heap of waste?
items.answer: Recyclers use strong magnets, often attached to cranes, to attract and separate iron articles (magnetic substances) from heaps of mixed waste materials.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Why is it necessary to separate substances from a mixture? Give one reason.
items.answer: Separation is necessary to remove undesirable or harmful components, or to obtain useful components from a mixture, making them fit for use or consumption.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What kind of substances can be separated using magnetic separation?
items.answer: Magnetic separation is used to separate substances that are attracted to a magnet (magnetic substances like iron) from those that are not (non-magnetic substances).

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Why would a farmer use a thresher machine instead of traditional threshing and winnowing?
items.answer: A thresher machine is more efficient as it performs both threshing (separating grains from stalks) and winnowing (separating grains from husk) simultaneously, saving time and labor.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: If you spill iron filings in sugar, which method of separation would be most effective and why?
items.answer: Magnetic separation would be most effective. A magnet can be used to attract and remove the iron filings, leaving the sugar behind, as sugar is non-magnetic.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Why can’t sieving be used to separate salt dissolved in water?
items.answer: Sieving separates solids of different sizes. When salt is dissolved in water, it breaks down into particles too small to be caught by a sieve.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Malli handpicked black peppers from his pulao. What was the basis for this separation?
items.answer: Malli separated the black peppers based on visible differences in colour (black peppers vs. other ingredients) and shape, making them easy to pick out by hand.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Give an example of a mixture from which two different but useful components are separated.
items.answer: Churning curd separates butter (useful for eating/ cooking) and buttermilk (useful as a drink), both of which are useful components.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Describe the method of winnowing. What kind of mixtures can be separated by this method? Give an example from daily life or agriculture.
items.answer: Winnowing separates heavier components from lighter ones using wind or by blowing air. The mixture is dropped from a height; lighter particles (like husk) are blown away, while heavier particles (like grains) fall vertically. It’s used for mixtures of solids with different weights, like separating wheat grains from husk by farmers.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Explain the processes of sedimentation and decantation with an example. When would you choose this combination of methods for separation?
items.answer: Sedimentation is when heavier, insoluble solids in a liquid settle at the bottom (e.g., mud in muddy water). Decantation is then gently pouring off the clear liquid from the top, leaving the sediment. This combination is used when an insoluble solid is mixed with a liquid and the solid is dense enough to settle quickly.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is filtration? Describe how you would use a filter paper and a funnel to separate mud from muddy water. What are the separated components called?
items.answer: Filtration separates insoluble solids from a liquid using a filter. To separate mud from water, fold a filter paper into a cone shape, place it in a funnel. Pour the muddy water through it. The mud particles (residue) will be trapped by the filter paper, and clear water (filtrate) will pass through into the container below.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Describe the method of evaporation for separating a solid dissolved in a liquid. How is this method used in obtaining common salt from seawater?
items.answer: Evaporation involves heating a solution so the liquid turns into vapour, leaving the dissolved solid behind. For salt from seawater, seawater is collected in shallow pits. The sun’s heat evaporates the water over days, and the solid salt remains. This salt is then collected and purified further.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Compare and contrast handpicking and sieving as methods of separation. Give one situation where each method is most suitable. (Evaluating)
items.answer: Both separate solids from solids. Handpicking relies on visible differences (size, colour, shape) and is suitable for removing small quantities of larger, distinct impurities (e.g., stones from rice). Sieving separates based purely on particle size difference using a mesh; suitable for separating finer particles from coarser ones (e.g., flour from bran).

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Imagine you have a mixture of sand, salt, and iron filings. Outline a sequence of methods you would use to separate these three components.
items.answer: First, use magnetic separation: pass a magnet over the mixture to remove the iron filings. Second, add water to the remaining sand and salt mixture to dissolve the salt. Third, use decantation (after sedimentation) or filtration to separate the insoluble sand from the salt solution. Finally, use evaporation to recover the salt from the water.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: What is churning? Explain how this process is used in households to obtain butter. What property of butter allows it to be separated this way?
items.answer: Churning is the vigorous agitation of a liquid, typically curd or cream. In households, curd is churned using a mathni (churner). This process causes the fat particles (butter) to clump together. Butter, being lighter than buttermilk, floats on top and can be skimmed off.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Threshing machines perform both the tasks of threshing and winnowing simultaneously. Explain how this is beneficial for farmers.
items.answer: This is beneficial as it combines two laborious and time-consuming processes into one, increasing efficiency. Farmers can separate grains from stalks and husk much faster, reducing manual effort, saving time, and potentially leading to quicker processing of the harvested crop and reduced crop loss.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: Why is it important to separate components from a mixture? Give at least two distinct reasons with examples.
items.answer: 1. To remove unwanted or harmful components : For example, separating small stones from rice before cooking makes the rice safe and pleasant to eat.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: When preparing meethi puri, Valli’s Mami sieved the wheat flour. What was she trying to remove, and why is this step important before kneading the flour?
items.answer: Valli’s Mami was trying to remove bran and any small impurities or coarse particles that might be present in the wheat flour. This step is important to ensure the flour is fine and clean, resulting in a smoother texture for the meethi puri and removing any undesirable elements.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: At a construction site, workers need to separate pebbles and small stones from sand before mixing cement. They have a large wire mesh screen mounted on a frame. They shovel the mixture of sand, pebbles, and stones onto the screen. (i) What method of separation are the workers using? (ii) What property of sand, pebbles, and stones allows this separation method to work? (iii) What happens to the sand, and what happens to the pebbles and stones during this process?
items.answer: (i) The workers are using the method of sieving. (ii) The different sizes of the particles (sand being fine, pebbles and stones being coarser) allow this method to work. (iii) The finer sand particles pass through the holes of the wire mesh screen, while the larger pebbles and stones remain on top of the screen.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: A person accidentally spills tea leaves into a cup of freshly brewed tea. They do not have a tea strainer available immediately. They decide to let the cup sit undisturbed for a few minutes. (i) What will likely happen to the tea leaves if the cup is left undisturbed? Name this process. (ii) What method can the person then use to pour out most of the clear tea, leaving the leaves behind? (iii) Will this method completely remove all tea leaves? What could be used for better separation? (Evaluating)
items.answer: (i) The heavier tea leaves will likely settle down at the bottom of the cup. This process is called sedimentation. (ii) The person can use decantation, carefully tilting the cup to pour the clear tea into another cup. (iii) No, decantation might not remove all the tea leaves; some smaller ones might still be poured out. A tea strainer (filtration) would provide better separation.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: To make cottage cheese (paneer) from sour milk, the milk is first curdled. The solid part (paneer) then needs to be separated from the liquid part (whey). A clean muslin cloth is often used for this. (i) What method of separation is being used when the curdled milk is poured through the muslin cloth? (ii) What is the role of the muslin cloth in this process? (iii) What are the two components obtained after this separation process?
items.answer: (i) The method of separation being used is filtration. (ii) The muslin cloth acts as a filter; its fine pores allow the liquid whey to pass through while retaining the solid paneer. (iii) The two components obtained are solid cottage cheese (paneer) as the residue and liquid whey as the filtrate.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: A recycling facility receives a large batch of mixed waste containing plastic bottles, iron cans, paper, and glass pieces. They use a large crane fitted with a powerful electromagnet. (i) Which items from the mixed waste will be attracted by the electromagnet on the crane? (ii) What is this method of separation called? (iii) Why are the plastic bottles, paper, and glass pieces not picked up by the electromagnet?
items.answer: (i) The iron cans will be attracted by the electromagnet on the crane. (ii) This method of separation is called magnetic separation. (iii) Plastic bottles, paper, and glass are non- magnetic materials and are therefore not attracted to the electromagnet.

items.chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
items.stem: A street vendor sells roasted peanuts. After roasting, he rubs the peanuts to loosen their thin red skins. He then uses a traditional winnowing tray (soop) to separate the skins from the peanuts, especially on a slightly breezy day. (i) What method is the vendor using to separate the peanut skins from the peanuts? (ii) Why does this method work for separating peanut skins and peanuts? (iii) Would this method be as effective in a completely closed room with no air movement? (Evaluating)
items.answer: (i) The vendor is using the method of winnowing. (ii) This method works because the peanut skins are much lighter than the peanuts. The breeze carries away the light skins, while the heavier peanuts fall down. (iii) No, this method would not be as effective in a closed room without air movement, as there would be no wind to blow away the lighter skins.
